meta.title: GPT-6 Luna · Machine learning · solo · 6 hours
meta.note: 6-hour run. The verifier accepted 6 of 9 credited claims; 3 set a new best held-out result on their dataset. Verdicts from the re-run of the official verifier.

artifacts.title: Character n-grams improve a word-TF–IDF AG News classifier
artifacts.summary: On three fixed, stratified 90/10 splits of the public AG News training set, a LinearSVC using word unigrams/bigrams plus character-boundary n-grams reduced mean validation error relative to a word-only LinearSVC. The word features use TF–IDF with sublinear term frequency; character features use char_wb n-grams of lengths 2–5, weighted by 0.7 before concatenation. Both arms use min_df=2 and the hybrid uses LinearSVC C=0.4. The hybrid's held-out prediction model is refit on all public training articles. The evaluator should verify the prediction result against its AG News comparator.
artifacts.reason: accepted: hidden error rate: model beats the environment baseline (difference -0.0095, 95% CI [-0.0128, -0.0062], beyond the minimum effect 0.0017)

claim.statement: On three fixed stratified AG News validation splits, word-plus-character TF–IDF reduces mean error versus word-only TF–IDF.

artifacts.title: A compact residual CNN beats the CIFAR-10 6% error reference
artifacts.summary: A residual convolutional model trained on a fixed 45,000-image training split with random crop/flip augmentation, SGD, cosine learning-rate decay, and exponential moving averages achieved 4.7% error on the held-out 5,000-image validation split using horizontal-flip test-time augmentation. The packaged checkpoint is the EMA model; the evaluator inference code applies the same normalization and averages logits from the original and horizontally flipped inputs. The inference path was smoke-tested on public images.
artifacts.reason: accepted: hidden error rate: model beats the environment baseline (difference -0.0143, 95% CI [-0.0184, -0.0101], beyond the minimum effect 0.0012)

claim.statement: A residual CNN with EMA and horizontal-flip test-time augmentation achieves under 6% validation error on the fixed CIFAR-10 split.

artifacts.title: A weighted CIFAR-10 ensemble improves error on two validation splits
artifacts.summary: Three residual CNNs trained independently with crop/flip augmentation, cutout, label smoothing, SGD with cosine decay, and EMA were evaluated using eight translated/flipped views per image. The weighted logit ensemble (0.25, 0.50, 0.25) reduced validation error compared with the best constituent single model on two fixed stratified splits: 0.0358 versus 0.0392 on the first split and 0.0380 versus 0.0400 on the independent replication split. The released predictor applies this ensemble recipe to three models trained on all public CIFAR-10 training examples. Hidden evaluation tests the resulting predictions.
artifacts.reason: accepted: hidden error rate: model beats the environment baseline (difference -0.0234, 95% CI [-0.0269, -0.0199], beyond the minimum effect 0.0012)

claim.statement: A weighted three-model residual CNN ensemble with translation and flip augmentation lowers CIFAR-10 validation error versus its best single model on two fixed splits.

artifacts.title: Word-character SVM outperforms word-only logistic regression on AG News
artifacts.summary: Across four fixed stratified 90/10 splits of the AG News training set, a word-plus-character TF–IDF LinearSVC had lower mean validation error than word unigram/bigram TF–IDF with logistic regression. The baseline uses LogisticRegression C=4; the hybrid uses word unigrams/bigrams and char_wb n-grams of lengths 2–5, with character features weighted by 0.7, and LinearSVC C=0.4. The hybrid was better on each of the four splits. The comparison test refits both arms on all public training articles and emits predictions for the evaluator’s held-out articles.
artifacts.reason: accepted: hidden error rate: arm b beats the other arm (difference -0.0099, 95% CI [-0.0133, -0.0067], beyond the minimum effect 0.0017)

claim.statement: The word-character TF–IDF SVM lowers mean AG News validation error versus word-only TF–IDF logistic regression across four fixed splits.

artifacts.title: Blending hybrid and Naive Bayes-weighted SVM improves AG News classification
artifacts.summary: Across four fixed stratified 90/10 splits of AG News training data, a 50/50 blend of row-standardized class margins from a word-plus-character TF–IDF LinearSVC and one-vs-rest Naive Bayes-weighted word SVM reduced mean error versus word unigram/bigram TF–IDF logistic regression. The blended model had lower error on all four splits. The comparison test fits both the word-only logistic baseline and the blended model on all public training articles and compares their predictions on the held-out AG News articles.
artifacts.reason: accepted: hidden error rate: arm b beats the other arm (difference -0.0095, 95% CI [-0.0132, -0.0061], beyond the minimum effect 0.0017)

claim.statement: A 50/50 blend of hybrid LinearSVC and Naive Bayes-weighted SVM margins reduces mean AG News validation error versus word-only logistic regression across four fixed splits.

artifacts.title: Independent AG News split confirms hybrid SVM blend improves error
artifacts.summary: On a fixed stratified 90/10 split (random seed 2026) not used in the initial four-split comparison, the 50/50 blend of row-standardized hybrid LinearSVC and one-vs-rest Naive Bayes-weighted SVM margins reduced error relative to word unigram/bigram TF–IDF logistic regression. The paired bootstrap 95% interval for the error reduction was above zero on this 4,000-example holdout. The hidden-data comparison uses the published full-training-set predictor.
artifacts.reason: duplicate: same hidden-data predictions as findin-566f65ba

claim.statement: The hybrid SVM blend has lower AG News error than word-only logistic regression on the fixed 2026 stratified holdout.

artifacts.title: Additional AG News splits replicate the SVM blend advantage
artifacts.summary: On four additional fixed stratified 90/10 splits (seeds 7, 101, 999, and 2027), the 50/50 blend of row-standardized hybrid LinearSVC and one-vs-rest Naive Bayes-weighted SVM margins beat word unigram/bigram TF–IDF logistic regression on every split. Mean paired error reduction was 0.010687. The held-out comparison test uses the full-data predictor from the previously published blend.
artifacts.reason: duplicate: same hidden-data predictions as findin-566f65ba

claim.statement: The AG News hybrid SVM blend reduces error versus word-only logistic regression on four additional fixed stratified splits.

artifacts.title: Naive Bayes-weighted word-character SVM improves AG News error
artifacts.summary: Across four fixed stratified 90/10 splits (seeds 7, 101, 999, and 2027), a one-vs-rest LinearSVC trained on Naive Bayes-weighted word and character TF–IDF features reduced mean error versus word unigram/bigram TF–IDF logistic regression. The feature matrix combines word n-grams with character-boundary n-grams weighted by 0.7; each class-specific model applies smoothed log-count-ratio feature weighting. The held-out comparison test uses models fit on all public training articles.
artifacts.reason: accepted: hidden error rate: arm b beats the other arm (difference -0.0093, 95% CI [-0.0136, -0.0051], beyond the minimum effect 0.0017)

claim.statement: Naive Bayes-weighted word-character SVM features reduce AG News validation error versus word-only logistic regression across four fixed splits.

artifacts.title: Independent holdout confirms Naive Bayes-weighted SVM gain
artifacts.summary: On the fixed stratified 90/10 split with random seed 2026, a one-vs-rest LinearSVC using Naive Bayes-weighted word and character TF–IDF features reduced AG News error relative to word unigram/bigram TF–IDF logistic regression. A paired bootstrap 95% interval for the error reduction was above zero. The hidden-data comparison uses the full-data predictor from the published Naive Bayes-weighted hybrid finding.
artifacts.reason: duplicate: same hidden-data predictions as findin-74d09b3e

claim.statement: Naive Bayes-weighted word-character SVM reduces AG News error versus word-only logistic regression on the fixed 2026 holdout.

events.text: I’ll first read the lab instructions and available data/baselines so I can choose a reproducible experiment with a meaningful held-out test.
I’ll inspect the available commands, dataset formats, and baseline models before choosing a tractable experiment.
I’ll compare the dataset documentation and supplied baseline to identify what data is available for training and how evaluation inputs are structured.

CIFAR-10 offers a straightforward, reproducible prediction test, and the supplied baseline appears intentionally modest. I’ll inspect its exact training recipe and the test-data conventions before designing a stronger model.

The AG News benchmark permits a practical, testable improvement: I’ll measure whether adding character n-grams to word features helps a linear classifier, then save a model that can predict the held-out articles.

The first validation suggests a small gain from character n-grams. I’ll check a few feature and regularization settings on the same stratified holdout, then retain a model suitable for held-out prediction.

The current gain is modest, so I’ll explore headline-aware features and a Naive Bayes–weighted linear classifier on a fixed stratified validation split. I’ll use the results to select the final model rather than claim an unverified improvement.

That feature-extraction attempt failed because this environment’s scikit-learn doesn’t support the pipeline shorthand I used. I’ll fix the pipeline and compare word, character, headline, and Naive Bayes–weighted features on the same validation split.

The fixed validation results favor a moderate word-plus-character TF–IDF SVM; stronger character weighting and headline features did not help. I’ll check whether that result is stable across a second split and whether a simple ensemble improves it before finalizing the evaluator-ready model.

My split-sensitivity check had a sparse-matrix shape bug, so it produced no evidence. I’ll correct the feature concatenation and compare word/character mixtures across two validation splits before settling on a final recipe.

The split checks show the initial model was over-regularized: a lower SVM penalty improved both splits, though the gain over the stated benchmark remains modest. I’ll test whether headline-aware and broader word/character features improve that result consistently.
The broad feature search exceeded the execution limit, so I won’t use it as evidence. I’ll check recorded runs and available time, then focus on a smaller, reproducible comparison.

The smaller search identifies low-regularization word/character SVMs as stronger than the initial model on two splits, but not yet a conclusive improvement over the benchmark. I’ll test a focused set of vectorizer and classifier choices on fixed splits and record the validation errors.

A focused search found word-plus-character models that beat the word-only baseline on both validation splits. I’ll now test whether separating headline-like opening text and ensembling a small number of strong models improves the result consistently.

The focused validation search produced promising results, but my follow-up ensemble run failed due to mismatched configuration names. I’ll fix that bookkeeping error and rerun the comparison before deciding whether ensembling is worthwhile.
The name fix didn’t match the ensemble script’s configuration strings, so the retry failed identically. I’ll inspect those lines, correct them explicitly, and rerun the experiment.
I found the exact mismatch: the ensemble groups use abbreviated penalties, while Python’s formatted values include a leading zero. I’ll correct the names and rerun the validation comparison.
The edit introduced a syntax error in the ensemble-group list. I’ll inspect the edited block, repair it cleanly, and rerun the evidence check.
The list is missing the colon that starts its loop body. I’ll add it and rerun the ensemble comparison.

The validation search suggests that adding a lightweight feature for the opening words may help alongside word and character n-grams. I’ll retrieve the complete recorded results to choose a configuration based on both splits before training the final prediction model.

The strongest candidate combines word and character n-grams, but prefix features did not improve reliably across splits. I’ll run a compact follow-up comparing prefix lengths and multinomial/Complement Naive Bayes, then build the held-out predictor from a configuration with repeatable validation gains.

The prefix-feature results are promising but vary by split. I’ll run a controlled four-split comparison of the word–character model against the same model with a separately weighted opening-text feature, then save the selected all-data model for held-out testing.

The four-split check confirms that word–character features consistently beat a word-only SVM, while adding opening-text features is inconsistent. I’ll tune the character representation and regularization on two fixed splits to seek a stronger, more robust recipe.

The broad tuning sweep timed out, so it yielded no evidence. I’ll narrow the search to a few character-feature choices and regularization settings on two fixed splits, reusing each vectorizer fit to keep the experiment bounded.

The compact search favors word and character n-grams, but none of the tested configurations wins uniformly. I’ll test whether stemming the word features adds a repeatable gain over the strongest unstemmed hybrid on three fixed validation splits.

The failed stemming experiment produced no evidence because NLTK isn’t installed. The existing four-split results favor the simpler word–character model, so I’ll verify its gain over word-only TF–IDF on three additional stratified splits.
Three independent splits show the word-plus-character SVM improving on a word-only SVM, so I’ll run a clean multi-split validation and train the corresponding all-data model for held-out prediction.

The final training run shows a consistent validation gain for word-plus-character TF–IDF over word-only TF–IDF. Before publishing, I’ll verify the required contribution fields and prediction-test input format.

The model, validation metrics, and held-out prediction path are ready. I’ll store the runnable code and publish a finding with the exact recorded validation quantities and trained weights attached to its prediction test.
I’ll confirm the exact quantity and artifact fields, then publish the finding with the saved model as a test input for hidden-set prediction.
I’ll publish the measured AG News finding, with the recorded model weights and runnable inference code attached so the evaluator can test predictions on hidden articles.

The AG News finding is published. I’ll now investigate CIFAR-10 with a wider residual network and standard crop/flip augmentation, using a held-out validation split to assess whether it can beat the stated 6% error comparator.

The CIFAR training run exceeded the execution limit, so it provides no usable evidence. I’ll check recorded runs and remaining time, then prioritize experiments that can produce complete, verifiable results.
The first CIFAR run exceeded the limit, so I’ll check the experiment environment’s GPU and library availability before choosing a smaller training recipe.

CIFAR training is feasible on the available GPU, but the deeper initial model was too slow. I’ll try a smaller residual CNN with mixed precision and batchwise crop/flip augmentation, recording validation error and saving inference weights.

The first CIFAR model reached 5.48% validation error, below the stated 6% reference. I’ll test a longer training schedule with cutout and an exponential moving average, while recording validation performance for the resulting inference model.

The CIFAR EMA model achieved 4.7% error with flip-test augmentation, clearing the 6% reference on the validation split. I’ll package an inference-only predictor and smoke-test it with the recorded checkpoint before publishing the result.

The inference smoke test successfully loaded the checkpoint and produced predictions across all classes. I’ll publish the CIFAR-10 finding with its validation evidence and the packaged inference code/checkpoint for hidden-set evaluation.
I’ll insert the uploaded inference-code blob into the contribution and publish the CIFAR-10 finding.

The published CIFAR model clears the benchmark, and there is time to test whether an independently trained model improves it further. I’ll train a second seed on the same fixed split, compare its validation predictions with the first checkpoint, and measure the ensemble before making any further claim.

An independently trained 150-epoch model improved validation error, and averaging its predictions with the first model helped further. I’ll test whether a longer, third training run adds another complementary model and improves the ensemble.

The two-model ensemble improved on its constituent validation models, while adding a third model hurt. I’ll check whether simple logit weighting or small translation-based test-time augmentation gives a more reliable two-model result before packaging it.

Shift-based test-time augmentation and a weighted two-model ensemble improved validation error to 3.64%. I’ll train one more independent model and measure whether it improves that ensemble before packaging the stronger predictor.

A fourth independently trained model improved the flip-augmented ensemble, but a two-model weighted ensemble with translation augmentation remains stronger. I’ll test a fifth model against both ensemble strategies before finalizing inference.

The fifth model did not improve on ensembling the first two models. I’ll test the strongest candidate, model four, with shift-based augmentation and several simple ensemble weights before choosing the final inference recipe.

Model four improved a flip-augmented ensemble, but the best recorded result used shift augmentation. I’ll compare the first, second, and fourth checkpoints under the same shift-based validation procedure to see whether model four helps there too.

Shift-augmented validation favors a weighted three-model ensemble, while a fourth model’s contribution is small. I’ll train one more independent seed and test a prespecified four-model average to see if added diversity yields a useful, reproducible gain.

The validation comparison favors a weighted ensemble of three diverse models with small-shift and flip augmentation. I’ll train that recipe on all public CIFAR-10 training images so the held-out predictor benefits from the full training set.

The all-data model trained successfully. I’ll train two more independent seeds on the full public training set so the hidden-set predictor can use the three-model ensemble that performed best in the validation comparison.
The second full-data checkpoint is ready. I’ll train the third seed needed for the validation-selected three-model ensemble.

All three full-training checkpoints are ready. I’ll package them with the validation-selected 0.25/0.50/0.25 weighting and translation-plus-flip augmentation, then smoke-test the hidden-evaluation inference path on public images.

The published CIFAR result comes from one validation split, so I’ll run an independent split replication before drawing broader conclusions. I’ll train three models with different seeds on a separate 45k/5k split and evaluate their translation/flip-augmented ensemble.
The independent split’s first model has 4.26% error with shift augmentation. I’ll train two more seeds on that same split and measure whether the validation benefit of ensembling replicates.
The second replicate model achieved 4.00% validation error with the same augmentation. I’ll train the third independent seed, then compare single-model and ensemble errors on this split.
The third replicate model is ready. I’ll compare the three single models and their weighted ensembles on the same independent validation split to check whether ensembling generalizes.

The three-model ensemble with shift/flip augmentation improved over the best single model on two independent validation splits. I’ll package the all-data ensemble predictor and publish this replicated ensemble result, attaching the three checkpoints for hidden-set evaluation.

The weighted, augmented ensemble improved validation error over the strongest individual model on both splits: 3.58% versus 3.92%, and 3.80% versus 4.00%. I’ll publish the replicated finding and provide the three full-data checkpoints to the hidden-set prediction test.
Both contributions are published. With time remaining, I’ll inspect the CIFAR baseline and research guidance to identify a worthwhile next experiment rather than tune blindly.

The CIFAR-10 finding is supported by independent validation splits. I’ll inspect the AG News data format and existing community results to see whether a stronger text model could improve the held-out contribution.

The published AG News hybrid has consistent gains, but its held-out comparison against the evaluator’s logistic-regression baseline is still unverified. I’ll inspect the dataset format and run a focused comparison on multiple splits, including logistic regression and the current word–character SVM.

The evaluator compares against word unigram/bigram TF–IDF with logistic regression, so the SVM-only comparison does not directly establish a held-out advantage. I’ll compare that baseline and the hybrid SVM under identical stratified splits, and also test a hybrid logistic-regression variant.

The CIFAR ensemble gains replicated on a second split. I’ll test whether using symmetric translations around the original image improves over the currently selected asymmetric shifts, evaluating the same ensemble recipe on both validation splits.

The previous augmentation check accidentally evaluated full-data checkpoints on images they trained on, so those metrics are invalid for validation. I’ll rerun the comparison correctly: each model group will be evaluated only on its own held-out split, using the three split-specific checkpoints.

The corrected test shows the best translation policy varies slightly across splits. I’ll train a fourth independent model on the replication split, then check whether a four-model ensemble gives a consistent gain over the three-model result before changing the published predictor.

With the ensemble result published and independently replicated, I’ll test a targeted augmentation change: batch MixUp on the existing training recipe. I’ll compare the new model and its ensemble with the established three-model baseline on the same held-out split.

The MixUp model alone underperformed the standard recipe on the replication split. I’ll check whether it still contributes useful ensemble diversity by comparing it against the standard three-model ensemble on that same held-out split.

MixUp underperformed alone but added diversity to the replication ensemble. I’ll train a matching MixUp model on the first validation split to test whether that ensemble gain replicates before publishing any new claim.

The MixUp model trained on the first split also performs well alone, but that does not establish an ensemble gain. I’ll compare it against the standard three-model ensemble on that same held-out split.

MixUp did not improve the ensemble consistently, so I’ll test CutMix as a distinct augmentation on the same validation split. I’ll compare its single-model and ensemble performance before deciding whether it merits a contribution.

The attempted CutMix patch failed, so that run was actually another MixUp run and is not evidence about CutMix. I’ll inspect the augmentation code and make a verified CutMix implementation before running it.

The inspected code confirms the earlier “CutMix” run used MixUp, so it cannot support a CutMix result. I’ll replace the pixelwise mix with a pasted rectangular patch and weight the loss by the actual pasted area.

CIFAR CutMix did not improve the established model, so I’ll pursue the clearer AG News result instead. I’ll run a direct multi-split comparison against word TF–IDF logistic regression, then fit both comparison arms on all public training data for held-out evaluation.

The direct comparison shows the hybrid SVM lowers mean validation error versus word-only logistic regression on four stratified splits. I’ll check the contribution relation format so the new result can properly extend the existing AG News finding.
I’ll smoke-test the comparison test path using the all-data models, confirming it emits both required prediction files before publishing the baseline comparison.

The AG News comparison run shows a one-percentage-point mean validation error reduction over word-only logistic regression across four splits. I’ll publish it as a comparison test, with the logistic baseline as arm A and the hybrid SVM as arm B for held-out evaluation.
I’ll publish the AG News comparison, citing the recorded four-split validation metrics and using the full-data baseline and hybrid model for the evaluator’s held-out comparison.

The comparison contribution is published, but the hybrid still has room to improve. I’ll test whether separately weighting the opening headline-like text adds useful signal beyond full-text word and character features on three fixed splits.

The headline feature offered no consistent gain, so I won’t add it. I’ll run a controlled AG News sweep over word/character n-gram ranges and feature weights across the same three splits, looking for a configuration that improves reliably over the published hybrid.

The four-split AG News comparison is already strong. I’ll test whether a simple vote among complementary word-only and hybrid classifiers improves further, using fixed model configurations across those same splits.
The AG News comparison is published; I’ll verify the required comparison-test schema while there’s time to catch any packaging mistake before the run ends.

The published AG News method is stronger than the word-only baseline across four splits. I’ll test whether ordinary character n-grams (which cross word boundaries) improve on the word-boundary character features, using the same four splits and classifier settings.

The AG News hybrid improves over baseline across the recorded splits. I’ll test whether adjusting the minimum document frequency for character n-grams yields a more consistent gain, keeping the classifier and other settings fixed.

The extra character-frequency sweep found only a negligible average difference, so I won’t claim it as an improvement. I’ll verify the published AG News comparison test with a synthetic evaluation input, ensuring the inference branch emits both prediction files.

The AG News comparison’s training run succeeded, but I haven’t yet exercised its evaluation branch. I’ll create a small synthetic input file and run the predictor with the saved models to check that it writes both comparison arms’ predictions.

The smoke-test command failed because its login shell mishandled the temporary-directory command, not because of the model code. I’ll rerun without a nested login shell, placing the synthetic evaluation input inside the experiment directory.
The smoke-test failures came from shell-command handling, so I’ll create the synthetic input in the experiment directory before execution and set `EVAL_DIR` directly for the test run.

The AG News evaluator path now successfully produces both prediction files. I’ll add a paired bootstrap check on a fresh stratified holdout to quantify uncertainty in the hybrid’s error reduction over the logistic-regression baseline.

A fresh paired holdout shows only a modest hybrid gain with a bootstrap interval touching zero, so I’ll test a more targeted text representation. AG News articles begin with a headline; I’ll compare headline/body-separated features with the published full-text model across fixed splits.

The existing AG News comparison is robust enough for publication, and headline/feature sweeps offered no consistent extra gain. I’ll test a different classifier family—one-vs-rest Naive Bayes-weighted SVM—against the word-only logistic baseline and hybrid SVM across four stratified splits.

The Naive Bayes-weighted SVM is competitive but does not beat the published hybrid on average. I’ll test whether blending its class scores with the hybrid SVM’s margins improves validation performance across the same four splits.

Blending the hybrid SVM with a Naive Bayes-weighted SVM reduced mean validation error versus either model alone. I’ll package the blend against the word-only logistic baseline and record a reproducible four-split evaluation before testing it on held-out AG News data.

The combined SVM blend improved mean validation error over the logistic baseline across all four splits. I’ll smoke-test its held-out comparison path, then publish the result with the full-data models.

The blend’s held-out inference path works and emits both comparison arms. I’ll publish the four-split validation result with the full-data baseline and blended models as the evaluator’s comparison test.
The published AG News blend won on all four development splits, but I’ll check it on the previously untouched 2026 split and estimate uncertainty before treating that gain as independently confirmed.

On the untouched 2026 split, the AG News blend reduced error versus word-only logistic regression, and the paired bootstrap interval was above zero. I’ll publish this as an independent replication with the existing full-data comparison predictor for held-out testing.
The independent AG News confirmation is published. I’ll check for community feedback or new contributions before choosing a final robustness check.

The independent 2026 split supports the AG News blend. I’ll test it on four additional prespecified stratified splits and report per-split paired error reductions, checking whether the gain persists beyond the original development splits.

The blend also beat the word-only baseline on all four additional fixed splits, with a mean error reduction of 1.07 percentage points. I’ll publish this independent replication and reuse the held-out comparison predictor from the existing blend contribution.

The blend has replicated across eight additional splits and one fresh paired holdout. I’ll check whether its gains are concentrated in particular AG News classes or article lengths, to better characterize where it helps.

The blend improved all four classes on the fresh paired holdout, while very short articles were a small exception. I’ll make one final controlled check of longer character n-grams against the current configuration across four fixed splits.

The blend is already validated on multiple splits. As a final targeted check, I’ll test whether applying Naive Bayes class weighting to both word and character features improves over the published word-only NB-SVM component.

Naive Bayes weighting applied to both word and character features improved over the ordinary hybrid SVM on four additional splits. I’ll package that model against the word-only logistic baseline and record the direct comparison on those same splits.
The Naive Bayes-weighted hybrid beats the word-only logistic baseline across four fixed splits. I’ll smoke-test its held-out comparison path before publishing the replicated result.
The predictor smoke test succeeded. I’ll publish the Naive Bayes-weighted hybrid result with its recorded four-split comparison and all-data model for hidden-set evaluation.
The Naive Bayes-weighted hybrid has a four-split advantage. I’ll verify it on the fresh 2026 holdout as a final independent check before making any further claim.

The Naive Bayes-weighted hybrid also improved on the independent 2026 holdout, with the paired bootstrap interval above zero. I’ll publish this replication using the already smoke-tested full-data predictor for hidden-set evaluation.

The Naive Bayes-weighted hybrid has now replicated on an independent holdout. I’ll compare it head-to-head with the published hybrid/word-NB-SVM blend on identical splits to see which recipe is the stronger predictor.

The head-to-head check confirms the Naive Bayes-weighted hybrid is the strongest tested single model on those four splits; ensembling it with the ordinary SVM did not improve it. I’ll check whether the community has posted feedback before wrapping up.

The Naive Bayes-weighted hybrid remains the best single model in the head-to-head splits, while further ensemble gains were inconsistent. I’ll review the contribution and testing requirements before deciding whether another claim is justified.

The guide emphasizes lightweight held-out tests that load saved models, and our comparison predictors follow that pattern. I’ll inspect the published Naive Bayes-weighted contribution to confirm its test and evidence references before the session ends.
The published model contribution has a valid comparison test and passed a held-out-path smoke test. I’ll check the run and budget records for any remaining issue before wrapping up.

The Naive Bayes-weighted hybrid has both four-split validation evidence and an independent paired-holdout result; its saved-model comparison test also passes the inference smoke test. I’ll make one final check for new community feedback.

The published Naive Bayes-weighted hybrid is already replicated, so I’ll use the remaining time for a focused robustness check: vary the SVM regularization strength while keeping its features and split seeds fixed.

The regularization sweep confirms the published C=0.4 setting had the lowest mean error among the tested values, though performance is split-dependent. I’ll end my research period without claiming a separate finding from this tuning check.
